newsitem.title: USA: Beat goes on for profitable newspapers at convention.
newsitem.headline: Beat goes on for profitable newspapers at convention.

text.p: Relishing their surging profits but wary of shrinking circulation, newspaper publishers gathered in Chicago on Monday to consider their battle to retain readers.

Sharp cost savings in the form of lower newsprint prices and a pullback from the trend toward broader geographical distribution of papers has helped lift profits for many of the nation's newspapers, Newspaper Association of America President John Sturm said in an interview.

The economy's long-term expansion has been reflected in growing advertising lineage, and some papers have benefited from increased readership as competitors -- particularly in the afternoon newspaper category -- have gone out of business.

But much in the same way television network executives have blasted Nielsen ratings for underestimating their viewership, the newspaper industry has taken issue with statistics that apparently show it to have fewer and less interested readers.
"It's as if they were counting how many televisions are sold," Sturm said.

Dismissing the opinion that circulation declines spell the eventual demise of newspapers, Sturm said that on average each newspaper is read by 2.3 people, and by more if papers reread in coffee houses are considered.

A more exacting study of 3,000 people conducted for the publishers group and the American Society of Newspaper Editors earlier this year found 76 percent of respondents used their daily newspaper as a source of news in the past week, against 88 percent who used local television news and 68 percent who listened to the radio for news. The survey had a margin of error of 3 percentage points, meaning results could vary that much either way.

While the survey showed younger age groups were less likely to get news from either newspapers or television, the demographics showed nearly two out of three people with annual incomes of at least $50,000 either read a newspaper or watched local television news.

Sturm acknowledged a general complaint that people feel they do not have time to read the newspaper. He attributed most of the decline in overall circulation to the demise of some afternoon papers and the decision by others to stop delivery outside their core circulation areas. In Houston, where the afternoon Post went out of business, the Chronicle won over many but not all of the Post's readers, he said.

The issues newspaper publishers wanted to address at the meeting were narrowing the "credibility gap" between all forms of media and the public, and the need for newspapers to become more "visually attractive" to readers, Sturm said.
Meanwhile, newsprint prices that soared last year to around $800 a ton have retreated to around $550 a ton, easing profit pressures because printing costs make up 20 percent of expenses.

"A lot of people made reinvestments (last year), replacing printing presses, which is a good indicator they feel good about the future," Sturm said of the 1,200 publishers attending the Chicago meeting.

Earlier this month, Gannett Co. Inc., the chain that owns USA Today, reported its first-quarter profit rose 52 percent to $135 million, or 96 cents a share. First-quarter profits at Knight-Ridder Inc. more than doubled to $46.4 million, or 49 cents a share. Knight-Ridder's papers include the Miami Herald and the San Jose (Calif.) Mercury News.

Profits from newspaper publishing were also strong at the New York Times Co. ; Tribune Co., publishers of the Chicago Tribune and other papers; and Dow Jones & Co., publisher of The Wall Street Journal.
Sturm said newspaper owners increasingly "see themselves as content purveyors, where information is disseminated in different ways.

"They see themselves much like the movie industry. ... Newspapers are first an Internet product, then stories are collated and faxed to specific customers in advance, or put on e-mail or an on-line service, then into the newspaper, then used in archival form," he said.
There was no doubt Microsoft Corp. Chairman Bill Gates, a scheduled speaker at the three-day meeting, would address such content packaging issues.
